Random Forest vs XGBoost vs Stacking — Ensemble Learning Comparison¶

Goal: compare a bagging ensemble (Random Forest), a boosting ensemble (XGBoost) and a stacking ensemble (RF + XGBoost + SVM/NB → Logistic Regression meta-learner) on two datasets, against simple single-model baselines, and interpret their strengths and limitations.

Dataset Type Rows Task
Sri Lanka "Rain Tomorrow" (simulated local weather, 13 districts, monsoon seasons) tabular, numeric + categorical 6,000 Will it rain tomorrow? (Yes/No)
SMS Spam Collection (UCI, real messages) free text → TF-IDF 5,572 spam / ham
Bonus: Colombo monthly rainfall (simulated) time series 432 months SARIMA vs RF vs hybrid SARIMA+RF (stacking idea)

The weather data is simulated (src/generate_data.py) following Sri Lanka's real monsoon pattern, because raw Department of Meteorology data is not openly downloadable. The SMS data is a real public dataset.

1.1 Train/test split and models¶

  • 80 / 20 stratified split, same seed for all models (fair comparison).
  • Preprocessing is inside each pipeline: median imputation + scaling for numeric, one-hot for categorical.
  • Baselines: Logistic Regression, single Decision Tree.
  • Ensembles: Random Forest (bagging), XGBoost (boosting), Stacking, plus CatBoost (boosting with native categorical handling) as an extra.

1.2 Is the difference real? — repeated cross-validation¶

A single test split can be lucky. We run 5 × 2-fold repeated stratified CV (10 fits per model) on the full data and compare F1 distributions. A paired t-test on the per-fold scores checks whether the gaps are significant (the folds are identical for every model, so the scores are paired).

In [6]:
cv = RepeatedStratifiedKFold(n_splits=2, n_repeats=5, random_state=SEED)
cv_scores = {}
for m in ["Logistic Regression", "Decision Tree", "Random Forest", "XGBoost", "Stacking"]:
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    cv_scores[m] = cross_val_score(make_pipeline(m, plan, 2), X, y, cv=cv, scoring="f1", n_jobs=1)
    print(f"{m:20s} F1 = {cv_scores[m].mean():.4f} ± {cv_scores[m].std():.4f}   ({time.perf_counter()-t0:.1f}s)")
cv_rain = pd.DataFrame(cv_scores)
ax = cv_rain.plot.box(figsize=(10, 4), title="Rain – F1 over 10 CV folds", rot=15); plt.show()

def paired(a, b, df):
    t, p = stats.ttest_rel(df[a], df[b]);  return f"{a} vs {b}: mean diff = {(df[a]-df[b]).mean():+.4f}, p = {p:.4f}"
for a, b in [("Random Forest", "XGBoost"), ("Stacking", "Random Forest"), ("Stacking", "XGBoost"),
             ("Random Forest", "Decision Tree"), ("XGBoost", "Logistic Regression")]:
    print(paired(a, b, cv_rain))

1.4 Effect of the number of trees / boosting rounds¶

Random Forest should plateau (more trees never hurts, only costs time). XGBoost can keep improving or start to overfit, depending on the learning rate.

3. Bonus — Hybrid SARIMA + Random Forest (stacking for time series)¶

SARIMA models the linear/seasonal monsoon pattern; a Random Forest is trained on SARIMA's residuals to learn the non-linear remainder. Final forecast = SARIMA + RF(residual). One-step-ahead forecasts over the last 36 months.

In [12]:
from hybrid_ts import run_hybrid
ts = pd.read_csv(ROOT / "data" / "colombo_monthly_rainfall.csv", parse_dates=["month"]).set_index("month")["rainfall_mm"]
preds, ts_scores, _ = run_hybrid(ts, test_size=36)
display(ts_scores.round(2))
ax = ts.iloc[-84:].plot(figsize=(13, 4), color="black", lw=2, label="Actual")
preds[["SARIMA", "Random Forest", "Hybrid SARIMA+RF"]].plot(ax=ax, style=":", lw=2)
ax.set(title="Colombo monthly rainfall – test-period forecasts", ylabel="mm"); ax.legend(); plt.show()

5. Interpretation, strengths and limitations¶

5.1 What the results say¶

Rain tomorrow (tabular, 6,000 rows)

  • All ensembles beat the single Decision Tree by a large margin (Random Forest +0.083 CV-F1, p < 0.001). This is the classic bagging effect: one deep tree has high variance; averaging hundreds of de-correlated trees removes most of it.
  • Random Forest, XGBoost, Stacking and CatBoost all land in a narrow band (hold-out F1 ≈ 0.78–0.79, AUC ≈ 0.88–0.89). CatBoost was best on the hold-out split (F1 0.794); Stacking was best in repeated CV (0.799 ± 0.005).
  • The hold-out ranking (XGBoost slightly above RF) flips under repeated CV (RF above XGBoost by 0.008, p ≈ 0.002). Differences below ~0.01 F1 are within split-to-split noise → never pick a winner from one split.
  • Logistic Regression is almost as good (CV-F1 0.793). The rain signal (humidity, cloud cover, pressure, season) is mostly additive, so a linear model is already close to the ceiling; ensembles only add the small interaction terms. The remaining ~20% error is weather noise that no model can explain from these features.
  • XGBoost with default settings is sensitive to the learning rate: with lr = 0.3, test F1 drops after 25 rounds (overfitting), while lr = 0.1 peaks around 100 rounds. Random Forest just improves slowly and plateaus — it is much harder to overfit by adding trees.
  • In the stacking model the meta-learner trusts RF most (weight ≈ 3.9), then SVM (≈ 1.7), XGBoost least (≈ 0.4) — XGBoost's probabilities were largely redundant with RF's, so stacking learned to down-weight it.

SMS spam (text, imbalanced 87% ham / 13% spam)

  • Accuracy is misleading here (a "always ham" model already scores 87%), so F1 on the spam class is the key metric.
  • Stacking is clearly the best: CV-F1 0.947 ± 0.006, vs Random Forest 0.930, Naive Bayes 0.914, XGBoost 0.907, LR 0.875. All stacking gaps are significant (p < 0.02), and stacking is also the most stable (lowest std).
  • Here stacking works because its base models are diverse: Naive Bayes (probabilistic, good on rare words), RF (bagging) and XGBoost (boosting) make different mistakes, and the meta-learner gives the largest weight to NB (≈ 6.2) and RF (≈ 5.7).
  • XGBoost is the weakest ensemble on text: with thousands of sparse TF-IDF columns and only ~600 spam examples in training, boosting trees overfit to individual tokens; it would need tuning (lower depth, more regularisation, scale_pos_weight).
  • XGBoost's top features (claim, txt, free, mobile, cash, urgent, win, 150p) are exactly the human-recognisable spam signals, which makes the model explainable.

Hybrid SARIMA + RF (time series)

  • SARIMA (RMSE 55.4) and the hybrid (RMSE 55.7, but lower MAE 36.2 vs 36.6) are practically tied; Random Forest alone is worst (RMSE 60.7) because it only sees lags and cannot model the seasonal structure as well.
  • The hybrid only helps when SARIMA's residuals still contain learnable non-linear structure; here most of the residual is noise.

5.2 Strengths and limitations¶

Random Forest (bagging) XGBoost (boosting) Stacking
Main idea Many deep trees on bootstrap samples + random feature subsets, majority vote Shallow trees added sequentially, each correcting the previous errors (gradient + regularisation) Meta-model learns how to combine different base models' predictions
Reduces Variance Bias (and variance via regularisation) Both – exploits model diversity
Strengths Robust with default settings, hard to overfit by adding trees, parallel training, works on mixed data, built-in feature importance Often the top accuracy on tabular data, fast (hist), handles missing values, rich regularisation, early stopping Best and most stable scores in this study (esp. text), can mix very different model types, automatically learns which model to trust
Limitations Large memory/model size, slower prediction, can't extrapolate, impurity-based importance is biased towards high-cardinality features Many sensitive hyper-parameters (learning rate, depth, rounds) – overfitted at lr = 0.3 here, weaker on very sparse high-dimensional text without tuning ~10–40× slower to train (internal 5-fold CV), hardest to explain, small gains if base models are similar, risk of leakage if not built with out-of-fold predictions
Use when You want a strong, low-effort baseline You can afford tuning and want maximum tabular accuracy Base models are diverse and the last 1–2% matters more than speed/interpretability

5.3 Limitations of this study¶

  • The weather datasets are simulated – the real meteorological signal will be noisier and more non-linear (which usually increases the advantage of ensembles over logistic regression). The code works unchanged on real Department of Meteorology CSV data.
  • Default/lightly-tuned hyper-parameters were used for all models; a tuned XGBoost (e.g. via RandomizedSearchCV + early stopping) could change the ranking.
  • Paired t-tests on repeated CV folds are optimistic (folds overlap); treat p-values as indicative only.
  • The spam data is from 2000s UK SMS; modern Sri Lankan SMS/email spam (Sinhala/Tamil/Singlish) would need new training data.

5.4 Conclusion¶

Ensembles consistently beat single trees. On clean, mostly-additive tabular data, Random Forest, XGBoost, CatBoost and Stacking are statistically very close – Random Forest gives the best accuracy-per-effort. On high-dimensional, imbalanced text, Stacking gives a clear and stable gain because its base learners are diverse. The choice is therefore a trade-off between accuracy, training cost and interpretability rather than one model "always winning".
